lessons.title: Active Participation, Inclusion, Resilience & Self-Concept
lessons.description: Four key concepts — what each means in care contexts, and how they support individuals to thrive and feel valued.
lessons.content_html:
Four Concepts That Underpin Quality Care

When individuals use health and social care services, they need more than physical support — they need to feel that they have a voice, that they belong, and that they can cope with life’s difficulties. Four interconnected concepts underpin this: active participation, inclusion, resilience, and self-concept. Understanding each one — and how they differ — is essential for any learner in health and social care.

Active Participation

Active participation is about ensuring that individuals have a genuine say in how they live their lives and how their care is delivered. It is not enough for a practitioner to simply ask “is that alright?” — active participation means creating the conditions in which a person can meaningfully contribute to decisions about their own support.

Consider a resident at Ferndale Care Home, 81-year-old Mr Osei, who has mild cognitive impairment. Active participation means his key worker sits with him each week to discuss which activities he would like to join, what time he prefers his personal care, and whether he wants family visits on the weekend. His preferences are recorded in his care plan and staff follow them. Mr Osei is not a passive recipient of care — he is an active participant in shaping it.

Key Fact

Active participation is about the individual having a say in their own care and life decisions. It is distinct from inclusion, which is about equal access for all. Both are essential in person-centred care but they address different things.

Inclusion

Inclusion goes beyond treating people fairly — it means actively ensuring that every individual can access services, opportunities and community life on an equal basis, regardless of their disability, culture, language, age, or any other characteristic. Inclusion is about removing barriers rather than simply tolerating difference.

At Riverside Mental Health Support Service, a young woman named Priya, 22, has a severe social anxiety disorder. If staff only offer group therapy sessions, Priya is effectively excluded from support. An inclusive service would offer one-to-one appointments, video consultations, or written communication options so that Priya can access the same quality of care as other service users. Inclusion means no one is shut out.

It is a common misconception that active participation and inclusion are the same thing. They are related but distinct: active participation is about having a say; inclusion is about having equal access. An exam question that asks students to explain both concepts must treat them as separate ideas with separate explanations.

Barriers to inclusion can be physical (a GP surgery without wheelchair access), communicative (no British Sign Language interpreter available), attitudinal (staff making assumptions based on a person’s age or ethnicity), or systemic (referral pathways that exclude those without a fixed address). Care providers are legally required under the Equality Act 2010 to make reasonable adjustments to ensure equal access. From a health and social care perspective, inclusion is also an ethical obligation — individuals who are excluded from services experience worse health outcomes, greater isolation, and lower levels of well-being.

Resilience

The specification defines resilience precisely: it is an individual’s ability to successfully adapt to life’s unexpected challenges, whether in the face of social disadvantage or other adverse conditions such as family or relationship problems, workplace worries, or financial difficulties. This definition is important because resilience is not simply “being tough” or “coping” — it is about adaptation, and the specification names the types of adversity that resilience must contend with.

Resilience is relevant in care settings because individuals often arrive having experienced significant adversity. A young person leaving foster care at 18, a patient newly diagnosed with a chronic condition, or an older adult who has recently been bereaved may all need support to build their capacity to adapt. Practitioners who understand resilience can work with individuals to develop strategies — rather than simply providing services that individuals remain dependent on.

Key Fact

Resilience is defined as an individual’s ability to successfully adapt to life’s unexpected challenges, either in the face of social disadvantage or other adverse conditions including family or relationship problems, workplace and financial worries. The word adapt — not just “cope” — is the key term.

Self-Concept

Self-concept describes how an individual thinks about, evaluates and perceives themselves. It includes both self-esteem (how much a person values themselves) and self-worth (their overall sense of who they are and what they are capable of). A positive self-concept is closely linked to a high level of emotional well-being.

Self-concept is not fixed — it changes across the lifespan and is shaped by experiences, relationships, and social contexts. A child who is consistently praised for their efforts develops a more positive self-concept than one who is frequently criticised. An adult who loses their job may experience a temporary dip in self-concept if their sense of identity was closely tied to their career. Understanding self-concept helps care practitioners support individuals whose experiences have led to a negative view of themselves.

These four concepts reinforce one another. When an individual is included in their community, they feel valued — this supports a positive self-concept. When they actively participate in decisions about their care, they develop a sense of control and agency — which builds resilience. An individual with a strong self-concept is better placed to adapt to adversity, because they believe in their own capacity to manage difficulties. Conversely, exclusion from services damages self-concept, lowers resilience, and reduces the individual’s ability to participate meaningfully in their own care. A practitioner who understands these links does not treat the four concepts as a checklist — they see them as a connected framework for promoting well-being.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A frequent error on questions about these four concepts is treating active participation and inclusion as the same idea. The command word ‘Explain’ requires you to give reasons for the difference, not just name two things. Write: active participation is about the individual having a say in their care (because this promotes their sense of agency and control); inclusion is about equal access for all (because it removes barriers that prevent individuals from using services). Use “because” and “therefore” to show the reasoning — that is what earns the third and fourth marks on a short explanation question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Active participation means individuals have a genuine say in their own care; inclusion means equal access for all regardless of need or background — they are related but distinct concepts.
  • Resilience is the ability to successfully adapt to life’s unexpected challenges, including social disadvantage and family, workplace or financial adversity.
  • Self-concept is how an individual thinks about and evaluates themselves; a positive self-concept supports high levels of emotional well-being and is shaped throughout life by experiences and relationships.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how self-concept is linked to resilience for individuals who use health and social care services.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies the link between self-concept (how individuals think about and value themselves) and resilience (adapting to adversity) with developed reasoning from at least two angles. Example content: a positive self-concept supports resilience because an individual who believes in their own capabilities is better placed to adapt when challenges arise; conversely, a negative self-concept (e.g. low self-esteem resulting from abuse or exclusion) can undermine resilience by making the individual feel unable to cope. May also explore the role of practitioner support in building both simultaneously. Uses 'because', 'therefore', 'this means that'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies the link with some development; may address only one direction of the relationship.

Developing (2 marks): Names both concepts but offers limited explanation of the connection.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one concept correctly with little or no link to the other.

practice_questions.text:
Fatima is 15 years old and lives in a residential children's home. She has experienced significant family disruption and has low self-esteem. She rarely joins in group activities and says she does not want to be involved in any decisions about her care.

Analyse how the key worker at the home could use active participation, inclusion and an understanding of resilience to support Fatima's well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Chains the analysis across all three concepts with reference to Fatima's specific circumstances. Example content: Active participation — the key worker could begin with small, low-pressure choices (e.g. what to eat for breakfast) rather than large care-plan decisions, because Fatima's low self-esteem means being asked to make major decisions immediately could feel overwhelming, therefore gradually building her sense of agency. Inclusion — offering one-to-one alternatives to group activities means Fatima is not excluded simply because of her preference, because inclusion requires removing barriers not insisting on conformity. Resilience — by praising small achievements and reflecting on past difficulties Fatima has managed, the key worker helps her recognise her own capacity to adapt, because resilience is built through experience of overcoming adversity with support. Candidate shows how the three concepts interact: active participation builds agency, agency supports resilience, inclusion ensures Fatima feels valued and her self-concept improves.

Secure (5–6 marks): Addresses all three concepts with mostly developed reasoning; some reference to Fatima's circumstances.

Developing (3–4 marks): Addresses two concepts with some development; links to Fatima's circumstances are partial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names concepts with little development or application.

lessons.title: Factors Shaping Self-Concept & Strategies for Resilience
lessons.description: The twelve factors that shape self-concept and six evidence-based strategies for building resilience.
lessons.content_html:
What Shapes Self-Concept?

Self-concept — how an individual thinks about, evaluates and perceives themselves — is not fixed at birth. It is constantly shaped and reshaped by a wide range of factors throughout life. Some of these factors have a positive influence, strengthening an individual’s sense of worth and identity. Others have a negative influence, undermining self-esteem and making it harder for someone to see their own value. The specification identifies twelve factors that affect self-concept, and understanding how each one works — and how they interact — is central to this topic.

The Twelve Factors

The twelve factors can be grouped to make them easier to remember. The first group relates to personal characteristics and experiences: age, appearance, gender and sexuality. The second group relates to social and relational influences: relationships with others, culture and education. The third group relates to adversity and discrimination: abuse, stereotyping and discrimination, unconscious bias and social media. The twelfth factor — life experiences — acts as an overarching category that can encompass many of the others.

Key Fact

The twelve factors affecting self-concept are: abuse, age, appearance, culture, education, emotional development, gender, income, life experiences, relationships with others, sexuality, social media, stereotyping and discrimination, and unconscious bias. (Note: some versions of the spec list 12 distinct factors; always learn from the most recent published version and your notes.)

Positive and Negative Influences

Each factor can operate as a positive or negative influence depending on the individual’s circumstances. Stereotyping and discrimination almost always harm self-concept — when a person is repeatedly told, either explicitly or through others’ behaviour, that they are “less than”, they begin to internalise that message. Research consistently links experiences of racism, sexism or homophobia to lower self-esteem and poorer mental health outcomes.

By contrast, positive relationships with others are among the most powerful constructive forces on self-concept. When a parent consistently encourages a child, when a teacher notices and names a student’s strengths, or when a care worker treats a service user with genuine respect, the individual’s sense of their own worth is reinforced. Consider 14-year-old Daniil, who has just moved schools. His new form tutor regularly praises his contributions in class and pairs him with a supportive peer mentor. Within a few weeks, Daniil’s self-confidence has improved noticeably. Positive relationships at a critical life stage can offset the negative effects of other factors.

Age affects self-concept in different ways at different life stages. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable to self-concept fluctuations as they negotiate their identity. Older adults in later adulthood may face ageist assumptions about their capabilities — being spoken to slowly, being left out of decisions — which can damage their sense of self-worth.

Appearance is significant because society attaches value to physical looks, particularly in adolescence. A young person whose appearance does not match cultural ideals of attractiveness may experience lower self-esteem. Positive feedback about appearance from trusted people can counteract this.

Social media is a contemporary factor with significant negative potential. Constant comparison to curated, filtered images of others can lead individuals to feel their own lives or bodies are inadequate. For young people in particular, the social validation of likes and followers can become a measure of self-worth — making self-concept unstable and dependent on external approval.

Unconscious bias occurs when practitioners or peers make automatic assumptions about individuals based on characteristics such as race, gender or disability — without realising they are doing so. For the service user, repeated experiences of unconscious bias can lead to internalised negative self-concept: they begin to believe they are less capable or less valued than others.

How Factors Interrelate

The twelve factors do not operate in isolation. Income, for instance, affects the environment a person grows up in, the education they can access, their appearance (including the clothes and products available to them), and the relationships they are able to maintain. A child growing up in poverty may face multiple simultaneous negative influences on their self-concept. Conversely, strong emotional development — developed through secure early attachments — can buffer an individual against the harmful effects of other factors. Mark schemes on this topic often reward candidates who can identify two factors and explain how each affects self-concept, with examples.

Key Fact

Factors affecting self-concept can be positive (supportive relationships, educational achievement, positive life experiences) or negative (abuse, discrimination, social media comparison, unconscious bias). The same factor can work in either direction depending on the individual’s circumstances.

Six Strategies for Developing Resilience

Resilience — the ability to adapt successfully to life’s unexpected challenges — can be developed. The specification identifies six named strategies that support resilience-building. Practitioners in care settings use these strategies to help service users manage adversity more effectively.

1. Self-reflection and learning from past difficulties. Individuals who take time to reflect on how they have managed previous challenges begin to recognise patterns in their own resilience. A social worker might encourage a care leaver to think about a difficult transition they have already navigated and identify what helped them at the time.

2. Recognising personal strengths and qualities. Many individuals who have experienced adversity struggle to identify their own strengths. Practitioners support resilience by helping individuals name their capabilities — “you managed that difficult conversation really well; that took courage.” Recognising strengths provides a foundation for self-concept and for facing future challenges.

3. Positive interactions with others. Maintaining supportive relationships — with friends, family, peers or practitioners — provides the emotional scaffolding that helps individuals manage difficult times. Feeling heard and valued by others reinforces a positive self-concept, which in turn supports resilience.

4. Participating in new activities. Taking on new experiences — joining a sports club, starting a course, volunteering — builds competence and confidence. Each successful new experience adds to an individual’s evidence that they are capable, which strengthens both self-concept and the capacity to adapt.

5. Achievements, praise and rewards. External recognition matters, particularly during periods of low self-esteem. When a care worker acknowledges that a service user has reached a goal — however small — it reinforces positive self-concept and motivates continued effort. This is not about empty praise, but about honest recognition of genuine progress.

6. Understanding personal limits and setting realistic goals. Resilience is not about pushing through regardless of cost. Individuals who understand their own boundaries — who can say “I need a break” or “that is too much for me right now” — are less likely to experience burnout or crisis. Setting realistic, achievable goals means progress is possible and self-concept is maintained, rather than being repeatedly undermined by unachievable targets.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark question asking you to identify two factors affecting self-concept and explain how each works, the most common error is giving two factors that are so similar they cannot be awarded two separate marks — for example, “discrimination” and “stereotyping”, which are listed as one combined factor. Make sure your two chosen factors are genuinely distinct items from the list of twelve. Then for each factor, use the word “because” to show how it affects self-concept, not just that it does. For example: “Social media negatively affects self-concept because young people compare themselves to filtered images of others, leading them to feel inadequate, therefore lowering their self-esteem.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Twelve factors shape self-concept — including age, appearance, relationships, culture, income, abuse, social media, stereotyping and discrimination, and unconscious bias — and each can work positively or negatively depending on circumstances.
  • The six resilience strategies are: self-reflection on past difficulties, recognising personal strengths, positive interactions with others, participating in new activities, achievements and praise, and setting realistic goals.
  • Factors do not operate in isolation — income, education, relationships and emotional development interact, and high-tariff exam answers show how multiple factors compound each other.

Which of the following is one of the twelve factors that can affect self-concept?
A) Resilience
B) Active participation
C) Unconscious bias
D) Well-being
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconscious bias [1 mark]. Resilience, active participation and well-being are related concepts but are not listed among the twelve factors affecting self-concept.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which social media can negatively affect an individual's self-concept.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct, accurate points (max 2). Acceptable answers: constant comparison to filtered/curated images leads to feelings of inadequacy [1]; relying on likes and followers as a measure of self-worth makes self-concept unstable and dependent on external approval [1]; cyberbullying via social media platforms damages self-esteem [1]. Two near-identical points score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how stereotyping and discrimination can negatively affect a person's self-concept.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the effect (experiencing stereotyping or discrimination leads to lower self-esteem / negative self-concept); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because repeated messages that a person is inferior or 'less than' are internalised over time); 1 mark for a further development or example (e.g. therefore the individual begins to believe these negative messages about themselves, which affects their emotional well-being and their willingness to engage with education, employment or social opportunities).

practice_questions.text: Describe two strategies a key worker at a residential care home could use to help an older adult develop resilience following a bereavement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy, applied to the care home context. Example: Recognising personal strengths and qualities (2 marks) — 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for describing a specific key-worker action with reference to the care home setting (e.g. the key worker meets regularly with the resident to discuss a skill or quality they have demonstrated that week, such as showing patience during a physiotherapy session, so that the resident begins to recognise their own capabilities). Setting realistic goals (2 marks) — 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. agreeing with the resident that they will attend one group activity per week rather than expecting full re-engagement with social life immediately). Other strategies accepted with equivalent development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how two factors affecting self-concept can interact to produce a compounded negative effect on an individual's well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Selects two distinct factors from the twelve and explains each separately, then shows how they interact to produce a compounded effect. Uses 'because', 'therefore', 'this means that'. Example content: Income affects self-concept negatively because poverty restricts the individual's access to resources associated with social acceptance (clothing, activities, food) [1], therefore the individual may feel different from peers and develop low self-esteem [1]. Education interacts with income: a person from a low-income background may attend a school with fewer resources, limiting their academic achievement [1], which reduces their sense of capability and reinforces a negative self-concept [1]. Together, low income and limited educational achievement create a compounding effect — each factor makes the negative impact of the other worse, reducing the individual's overall sense of worth and future prospects [2].

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses both factors with some development; the interaction is identified but not fully explored.

Developing (2 marks): Describes both factors in isolation without showing how they interact.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one factor with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Kolade is 17 years old and has recently left care. He struggled at school, has a difficult relationship with his family, and has low self-esteem. He is now living independently in a supported housing placement. His support worker wants to help him develop a more positive self-concept and build resilience.

Evaluate how effectively the six resilience strategies could support Kolade's well-being in his current situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Selects at least four of the six strategies, evaluates each with specific reference to Kolade's circumstances (care leaver, low self-esteem, difficult family relationships, independent living), and makes a balanced overall judgement about effectiveness. Example content: Self-reflection — supports Kolade because care leavers have often managed significant adversity; reflecting on past difficulties he has overcome provides evidence of his own resilience [positive]; however, if reflection focuses primarily on failure (school struggles, family breakdown) without skilled facilitation by the support worker, it could reinforce negative self-concept [limitation]. Recognising personal strengths — highly relevant given Kolade's low self-esteem; the support worker's role is to identify and name strengths he cannot yet see himself [positive]. Participating in new activities — supported housing often provides opportunities for this; each successful new experience adds to Kolade's evidence of capability [positive]; however, anxiety or past rejection may make trying new things threatening [limitation]. Setting realistic goals — essential for Kolade, who may have experienced only unachievable targets in school; small, achievable milestones (e.g. attending college interview) protect self-concept [positive]. Conclusion: all six strategies have potential, but their effectiveness depends on the quality of the support worker relationship and Kolade's readiness to engage. The strategies work best in combination, not isolation.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strategies with relevant reference to Kolade; some evaluation of effectiveness.

Developing (3–5 marks): Describes some strategies with limited evaluation; application to Kolade is partial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names one or two strategies with minimal application.

lessons.title: Defining Health, Illness, Disease & Well-being
lessons.description: Compare definitions of health, illness, disease and well-being and how they overlap.
lessons.content_html:
Why Definitions Matter

In health and social care, precise language is essential. The words “health”, “illness”, “disease” and “well-being” are used by practitioners every day — but they do not all mean the same thing. The exam unit requires you to know four specific definitions, each drawn from a named authoritative source. These definitions are not interchangeable, and mark schemes credit only candidates who can distinguish between them accurately. This lesson covers each definition in turn, explains its source, and explores the interpretive layers that the exam also assesses.

Health — The WHO Definition

The most widely used definition of health comes from the World Health Organization (WHO). The WHO defines health as “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.” This definition was established in 1948 and remains the standard reference point for practitioners and policymakers.

Three features of this definition are particularly important for the exam. First, it is holistic — it covers physical, mental and social dimensions, not just the physical body. Second, it goes beyond the absence of disease: a person may be free from identifiable illness but still not be healthy if their mental or social well-being is poor. Third, it uses the phrase “complete” well-being, which implies a high standard — a standard that some argue is rarely achievable in practice.

Key Fact

The WHO (1948) defines health as: “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.” The key phrase is not merely the absence of disease — health is a positive state, not just the lack of illness.

Illness — A Personal Experience

While the WHO definition of health is a professional, objective standard, illness is defined quite differently. Drawing on the British Medical Journal, the specification frames illness as the feeling or experience of ill health — a subjective state that is personal to the individual. This is a crucial distinction: illness is what a person feels, not what a test detects.

The significance of this definition is illustrated by two scenarios. First, illness without disease: a person may feel genuinely unwell — fatigued, in pain, anxious — but no physical cause can be found by medical tests. The person is experiencing illness even though no disease is present. Conditions such as medically unexplained symptoms, chronic fatigue syndrome or certain forms of chronic pain fall into this category. Second, the reverse is also possible: a person may have a diagnosed disease (for example, early-stage hypertension) but feel completely well in themselves. In that case, disease is present without the individual experiencing illness.

In a care setting, a practitioner who only acts when a medically confirmed disease is present may fail to support individuals experiencing genuine illness. A person who says they feel exhausted, anxious and unable to cope deserves to be taken seriously even if blood tests come back clear. Equally, a person with a confirmed chronic condition may not feel “ill” on a daily basis and may not want to be treated as unwell. Person-centred care requires practitioners to respond to both the objective condition and the subjective experience of health.

Disease — Signs and Symptoms

Disease is defined by the specification as a condition characterised by specific signs and symptoms. Unlike illness, which is subjective, disease is an objective, clinically identifiable state. Signs are what a practitioner can observe or measure — a rash, an elevated white blood cell count, a raised temperature. Symptoms are what the patient reports feeling — pain, breathlessness, nausea. A disease can typically be named (for example, pneumonia, type 2 diabetes, multiple sclerosis) and diagnosed through clinical assessment or testing.

It is important to remember that an individual can have a disease without experiencing illness (as in the early-stage hypertension example above), and can experience illness without having a diagnosable disease. Examiners test this distinction — knowing only the general meaning of each word is not enough. You need to be able to explain the specific conceptual difference and give an example that illustrates it.

Key Fact

Illness is the personal, subjective experience of feeling unwell — you can have illness without disease. Disease is an objective, clinically identified condition with specific signs and symptoms — you can have disease without experiencing illness. The two do not always go together.

Well-being — More Than Feeling Fine

The fourth definition — well-being — draws on Psychology Today’s definition. Well-being is described as being happy, healthy and thriving, with good mental health, high life satisfaction, a sense of purpose, and the ability to manage stress. Like the WHO definition of health, well-being is a broad, positive concept — it is about flourishing, not merely the absence of problems.

Well-being differs from health in that it places greater emphasis on the subjective sense of thriving. A person can be medically healthy in the WHO sense but still have low well-being if they feel their life lacks purpose or if they are chronically stressed. This distinction is relevant in care settings: practitioners promoting well-being are not just treating illness or disease — they are supporting individuals to flourish and find meaning.

A holistic view of health recognises that what it means to be “healthy” or to have “well-being” is not universal. These concepts vary between cultures (some cultures prioritise collective harmony over individual health; others integrate spiritual health into their understanding of well-being), across time (historical understandings of health were very different from today’s biomedical model — Victorian medicine did not recognise mental illness in the same way), and across life stages (a 3-year-old’s well-being is largely about attachment and play; a 75-year-old’s well-being may be more about autonomy, social connection and freedom from pain). Practitioners who appreciate this variation are better placed to provide genuinely person-centred care.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Mark schemes for questions on these four definitions often carry a source attribution requirement — candidates who name the WHO for health, the British Medical Journal for illness, and Psychology Today for well-being earn additional credit. Practise writing all four definitions in one sitting and including the source each time. A common error is to define ‘well-being’ using the WHO definition of health, or to use “illness” and “disease” as if they mean the same thing. The command word ‘Describe’ on a 2-mark question expects the core meaning plus one relevant detail; ‘Explain’ on a 3-mark question requires you to give a reason why the definition matters, using “because” or “therefore”.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health (WHO, 1948): a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. A holistic, positive concept that covers three dimensions.
  • Illness (British Medical Journal): the personal, subjective feeling of being unwell. Can exist without disease; disease can exist without illness. The two do not always coincide.
  • Well-being (Psychology Today): being happy, healthy and thriving — with good mental health, high life satisfaction, a sense of purpose and the ability to manage stress. Varies across cultures, time and life stages.

lessons.title: Physical Indicators of Health & Interpreting Data
lessons.description: Measure pulse, blood pressure, BMI, peak flow and temperature, then interpret the results.
lessons.content_html:
Why Physical Indicators Matter

Health professionals use physical indicators of health to move beyond what a person says they feel. While illness is a subjective experience, physical indicators provide objective, measurable data that can be compared against established normal values and tracked over time. The specification identifies five physical indicators that students must know: blood pressure, peak flow, body mass index (BMI), waist-to-hip ratio, and pulse rate (both resting and recovery after exercise).

Interpreting these indicators is not simply about checking whether a number falls within a range. It requires understanding patterns and trends in data, identifying increases, decreases, similarities and differences, and then considering the contributing factors that might explain those patterns. The four named contributing factors are: age, sex, lifestyle and environment.

Blood Pressure

Blood pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer and expressed as two figures — systolic pressure (when the heart contracts) over diastolic pressure (when the heart rests between beats) — in millimetres of mercury (mmHg). The ideal reading for a healthy adult is around 120/80 mmHg. A reading of 140/90 mmHg or above is classified as hypertension (high blood pressure), which significantly raises the risk of heart disease, stroke and kidney damage. Readings consistently below 90/60 mmHg indicate hypotension (low blood pressure), which can cause dizziness and fainting.

Key Fact

Ideal adult blood pressure: 120/80 mmHg. Hypertension threshold: 140/90 mmHg or above. Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart disease and stroke. Many people have hypertension without experiencing any symptoms — this is why regular monitoring matters.

Peak Flow

Peak flow is measured using a peak flow meter and records the maximum speed at which a person can blow air out of their lungs, in litres per minute (L/min). It is particularly useful for monitoring conditions affecting the airways, such as asthma. Unlike blood pressure, there is no single universal “normal” range for peak flow — expected values vary significantly by age, height and sex. A healthy adult male of average height will have a higher expected peak flow than a child or an older adult. Practitioners always compare an individual’s reading against a personal best or predicted value based on their specific characteristics.

A reading significantly below the individual’s personal best or predicted value suggests that the airways are narrowed or inflamed. In an asthma patient, a peak flow that is 50% or below their usual reading signals a severe attack requiring immediate treatment. Trends over time — such as consistently falling peak flow in the morning — provide more useful clinical information than a single reading.

Body Mass Index (BMI)

Body mass index (BMI) is calculated by dividing a person’s weight in kilograms by the square of their height in metres: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)2. The NHS uses four categories to interpret BMI in adults: under 18.5 is underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 is healthy weight; 25 to 29.9 is overweight; 30 and above is obese.

The exam focuses on interpretation rather than just category identification. A student who reads a BMI of 32 and simply writes “obese” will not access the higher marks. The mark scheme rewards candidates who link the reading to contributing factors — for example: “A BMI of 32 places this individual in the obese category. Contributing factors may include lifestyle (a diet high in processed foods and low physical activity levels) and environment (limited access to green spaces for exercise in the local area).” This value → category → contributing factor chain is the expected analysis pattern.

Key Fact

NHS BMI categories for adults: underweight < 18.5; healthy weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obese ≥30. BMI is calculated as weight (kg) divided by height in metres squared. Interpretation always considers contributing factors — age, sex, lifestyle and environment — not just the number itself.

A service user weighs 85 kg and is 1.70 m tall. To calculate BMI: 1.70 × 1.70 = 2.89 (height squared). 85 ÷ 2.89 = 29.4 (rounded to one decimal place). A BMI of 29.4 falls in the overweight category (25–29.9). To interpret this for the exam: lifestyle factors (e.g. low physical activity, high-calorie diet), environmental factors (e.g. working a sedentary desk job, living in an area with few leisure facilities), or age-related changes in metabolism could all contribute. Note that BMI does not distinguish between muscle mass and fat mass, so it may overestimate risk for individuals who are very muscular. A practitioner would not rely on BMI alone.

Waist-to-Hip Ratio

Waist-to-hip ratio is calculated by dividing the waist measurement (in cm) by the hip measurement (in cm). It indicates how fat is distributed across the body. Fat stored around the abdomen (“apple-shaped” distribution) carries a higher health risk than fat stored around the hips and thighs (“pear-shaped” distribution). The NHS uses sex-specific guidelines: for men, a ratio above 0.90 indicates increased risk; for women, above 0.85. Higher waist-to-hip ratios are associated with raised risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

Pulse Rate — Resting and Recovery

Pulse rate is measured in beats per minute (bpm). The normal resting pulse rate for an adult is 60 to 100 bpm. A resting rate below 60 bpm (bradycardia) may be normal in a highly trained athlete but in others could signal a cardiac problem. A rate persistently above 100 bpm at rest is tachycardia and may reflect stress, anaemia, infection, or cardiovascular disease.

Recovery rate — how quickly the pulse returns to its resting level after exercise — is a measure of cardiovascular fitness. A healthier heart and cardiovascular system recover more quickly. A slow recovery rate after moderate exercise suggests poor cardiovascular fitness and may indicate a need for lifestyle change or further investigation.

The four named contributing factors that affect all physical indicators are: age (blood pressure and BMI tend to increase with age; peak flow decreases in older adults), sex (men and women have different expected ranges for several indicators, including waist-to-hip ratio and peak flow), lifestyle (diet, exercise levels, smoking and alcohol consumption all influence readings), and environment (air quality, access to green spaces, housing conditions, and workplace hazards can all affect physical health indicators). When interpreting data in the exam, always consider which of these factors might explain a reading that falls outside the normal range, rather than simply labelling it as “unhealthy”.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Interpretation questions in the exam typically present a table of readings for a named individual and ask you to comment on what the data shows. The most common error is simply identifying that a reading is above or below the normal range without explaining why this might be the case. Always follow the three-step pattern: (1) state the reading and compare it to the normal value; (2) classify it (e.g. hypertension, obese); (3) suggest at least one contributing factor from age, sex, lifestyle or environment that could explain the reading. For BMI calculation questions, show your working clearly: height squared first, then divide weight by the result — a correct method with an arithmetic error earns partial marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five physical indicators are blood pressure (ideal 120/80 mmHg; hypertension ≥140/90), peak flow (varies by age/height/sex — compare to personal best), BMI (underweight <18.5; healthy 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obese ≥30), waist-to-hip ratio (cardiovascular risk above 0.90 for men, 0.85 for women), and pulse rate (resting adult 60–100 bpm).
  • Data must be interpreted against normal values and comparative data, with attention to patterns, trends, and possible contributing factors: age, sex, lifestyle and environment.
  • A single reading in isolation is less meaningful than a trend over time. Practitioners never rely on one indicator alone — they look for a pattern across multiple measures.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows three physical indicator readings for Marcus (46 years old, male, desk job, smokes 10 cigarettes per day):

Blood pressure: 148/96 mmHg
Resting pulse rate: 88 bpm
BMI: 31.2

Analyse what this data suggests about Marcus's health, using your knowledge of normal values and contributing factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Addresses all three indicators, compares each to normal values, correctly classifies each, and chains analysis through at least two contributing factors linked to Marcus's specific circumstances. Blood pressure: 148/96 mmHg is above 140/90 — hypertension [1]; this is a significant risk for heart disease and stroke [1]. Resting pulse: 88 bpm is within the 60–100 bpm normal range for adults, though at the upper end; Marcus's sedentary job and smoking may mean his cardiovascular fitness is poor [1]. BMI: 31.2 places Marcus in the obese category (≥30) [1]. Contributing factors: age (46 — metabolic rate slows in middle adulthood, making weight gain more likely) [1]; lifestyle (smoking raises blood pressure and reduces cardiovascular fitness; sedentary desk job reduces calorie expenditure) [1]; environment (desk job = prolonged sitting; may have limited access to exercise during working day) [1]. Analysis chains: his elevated BMI and sedentary lifestyle contribute to his high blood pressure; smoking compounds this by reducing arterial flexibility. A practitioner would not look at readings in isolation but recognise that multiple indicators suggesting poor cardiovascular health represent a compounded risk [1].

Secure (5–6 marks): Addresses at least two indicators correctly with some contributing factor analysis linked to Marcus.

Developing (3–4 marks): Addresses one or two indicators; limited contributing factor analysis.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Identifies a reading as high or low with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of BMI as a physical indicator of health for health professionals working in a primary care setting.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation identifying specific strengths of BMI (easy to calculate from height and weight, provides a consistent basis for comparison across populations, linked to clear risk thresholds for conditions such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, widely used and understood by practitioners) alongside specific limitations (does not distinguish between fat mass and muscle mass so may overestimate risk in muscular individuals; does not indicate fat distribution — waist-to-hip ratio is better for this; expected ranges may not apply equally across ethnic groups; does not capture mental, social or other dimensions of health; a single reading is less informative than a trend). Evaluates in context of primary care: a GP may use BMI as a quick initial screening tool but would combine it with other indicators (blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, lifestyle information). Reaches a reasoned conclusion: BMI is a useful starting point but should never be the only measure used, because its limitations can lead to misclassification. An effective evaluation gives specific examples and avoids purely listing pros and cons without linking them.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some development and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Notes some strengths and limitations with limited development.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very general response with no conclusion.

lessons.title: Promoting Health & Well-being — Role, Purpose & Supporting Individuals
lessons.description: Why health promotion matters, who delivers it, and how it supports individuals to change.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Health Promotion?

Health promotion covers the full range of activities — from a leaflet in a GP waiting room to a national television campaign — that are designed to improve the health and well-being of individuals and communities. In health and social care, understanding the role and purpose of health promotion is not just a theoretical exercise: practitioners at every level are involved in promoting health, whether they are a support worker encouraging a service user to walk more, a school nurse delivering a healthy eating session, or a community health champion running a stop-smoking group.

The Role and Purpose of Health Promotion

The specification identifies four overlapping purposes of health promotion. First, health promotion aims to raise awareness of health and well-being issues — many people do not know, for instance, that they may have high blood pressure, or that they are drinking more alcohol than is safe. Raising awareness through campaigns, screenings and information is the foundation of any health promotion effort.

Second, health promotion aims to increase individuals’ positive lifestyle choices. It is not enough to tell people that smoking is harmful; effective health promotion provides the information, motivation and practical support needed for someone to quit. The goal is to shift from knowledge to behaviour change — from knowing that exercise is good to actually doing it regularly.

Third, health promotion works to reduce risks to health and well-being. By encouraging vaccination, safer sexual practices, reduced alcohol consumption, and regular physical activity, health promotion addresses the major modifiable risk factors for the UK’s most common chronic conditions, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers.

Fourth — and this is the angle that is specific to this qualification and often tested — health promotion aims to reduce health and social care costs. A person who develops type 2 diabetes because of a preventable lifestyle factor will require ongoing NHS treatment, medications, and potentially social care support in later life. Every person who makes a positive lifestyle change, or who is screened and treated early, reduces the demand on publicly funded services. Health promotion is therefore not only a moral priority but an economic one.

Key Fact

The four purposes of health promotion are: raise awareness of health issues; increase positive lifestyle choices; reduce risks to health and well-being; and reduce health and social care costs. The cost-reduction purpose is frequently tested — prevention is cheaper than treatment.

Supporting Individuals to Take Responsibility

One of the most significant shifts in modern health and social care has been the move towards supporting individuals to take responsibility for their own health and well-being, rather than treating them as passive recipients of services. This approach recognises that lasting behaviour change is more likely when the individual is an active participant in their own health journey — not when they are simply told what to do.

Supporting individuals to take responsibility involves three main strategies. The first is prevention and control — providing individuals with the information and tools they need to prevent health problems before they arise or to manage existing conditions effectively. A GP practice running a pre-diabetes prevention programme, or a district nurse teaching a diabetic patient how to monitor their own blood glucose, are both examples of this approach.

The second strategy is educating by providing information and advice. This includes face-to-face consultations with health professionals, written materials such as leaflets and health promotion booklets, online resources, and community health events. The purpose of education is to equip individuals with the knowledge they need to make positive lifestyle choices — but providing information alone is rarely enough. Individuals also need to feel that the changes are achievable and relevant to their own lives. A health professional who provides culturally appropriate information, in a person’s first language, and at the right literacy level, is more likely to enable behaviour change than one who hands over a generic leaflet.

The third strategy is encouraging individuals to utilise their own strengths and informal networks. Rather than creating dependency on services, effective health promotion builds on what individuals already have — their social relationships, community connections, personal capabilities, and previous experience of managing difficulties. A person who is supported to recognise that they have already successfully made one health change (for example, cutting out sugary drinks) is more likely to believe they can make another. Informal networks — family, friends, faith communities, and workplace colleagues — can also be powerful sources of support for behaviour change.

Key Fact

Three strategies for supporting individuals to take responsibility: prevention and control (information and tools to prevent or manage conditions); educating through information and advice (knowledge that enables positive choices); and encouraging use of personal strengths and informal networks (building on what the individual already has rather than creating service dependency).

The Role of Campaigns, Education and Strengths-Based Approaches

At a national level, health campaigns are a key vehicle for raising awareness and enabling choice at scale. Campaigns such as Change4Life (now part of the NHS Better Health platform) and Stoptober reach millions of people through television, social media, GP surgeries and schools. Their power lies in their reach — no individual practitioner can achieve population-level impact alone.

At an individual level, a strengths-based approach in care settings shifts the focus from what a person cannot do to what they already can. A care worker using a strengths-based approach might ask: “What has helped you manage your health in the past?” and “Who in your life could support you with this?” This approach is consistent with the principles of active participation and person-centred care covered earlier in this unit — it treats the service user as the expert on their own life.

Health promotion operates at both local and national levels. At a national level, campaigns are coordinated by Public Health England (now the UK Health Security Agency) and NHS England, using mass media, social media, and GP referral programmes. At a local level, councils, GP surgeries, schools, voluntary organisations, pharmacies and community groups all play a role. For example, a local authority might fund a walking group for older adults, a school might run a mental health awareness week, or a pharmacy might offer free blood pressure checks. The most effective health promotion connects national campaigns with local delivery, so that the message reaches individuals in their own communities through trusted local contacts.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on promoting health and well-being often use the command word ‘Discuss’, which requires you to consider more than one angle — for example, both the benefits of health promotion (to individuals and to the health and social care system) and the challenges (individuals may not engage, campaigns may not reach all groups). Remember to include the ‘reduce health and social care costs’ purpose — this is frequently missed by students who focus only on the individual benefits. For 6-mark questions, aim to give two developed points from different perspectives, each using “because” or “therefore” to show the reasoning chain. A strong answer might contrast a national campaign approach with a strengths-based individual approach, noting what each does well and where each has limitations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health promotion has four purposes: raise awareness of health issues; increase positive lifestyle choices; reduce risks to health and well-being; and reduce health and social care costs. The fourth purpose is the most frequently tested in exam questions.
  • Supporting individuals to take responsibility involves three strategies: prevention and control; education through information and advice; and encouraging individuals to use their own strengths and informal networks rather than becoming dependent on services.
  • Effective health promotion combines national campaigns (which achieve population-level reach) with local delivery (which reaches individuals through trusted local contacts and person-centred approaches).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the four purposes of promoting health and well-being?

B) Reducing health and social care costs

practice_questions.marks: B) Reducing health and social care costs [1 mark]. Diagnosis, treatment plans and prescription access are clinical activities rather than health promotion purposes.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why health promotion is important for the NHS and social care sector.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct reasons (max 2). Acceptable answers: health promotion reduces demand on NHS services by preventing conditions before they develop [1]; health promotion reduces the long-term costs of treating preventable chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes [1]; raising awareness means conditions are identified and treated earlier, reducing severity and therefore the level of care needed [1]; enabling positive lifestyle choices reduces the number of people who develop conditions linked to modifiable risk factors [1]. Two near-identical points score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'strengths-based approach' to supporting individuals to improve their health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core meaning (identifying and building on the individual's existing strengths, capabilities and resources rather than focusing on deficits); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because individuals are more likely to sustain behaviour change when they feel capable and are using resources they already have); 1 mark for a specific practical example (e.g. a health worker asks a service user what has helped them manage their health successfully in the past and encourages them to use those same strategies rather than relying solely on professional support).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a GP surgery could use two different strategies to support patients to take responsibility for their own health and well-being.

Encouraging use of personal strengths and informal networks (2 marks): 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. the GP asks the patient who in their household or friendship group could walk with them regularly, helping them identify a support network that already exists rather than referring them to a paid service). Prevention and control also accepted with equivalent development.

practice_questions.text:
Sanjay is 52 years old and works in a call centre. He was recently told his blood pressure is borderline high and his BMI is 28.1. His GP wants to support him to make lifestyle changes rather than immediately prescribing medication.

Discuss how the GP could use health promotion strategies to support Sanjay to take responsibility for his own health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Addresses at least two health promotion strategies with developed reasoning, both linked to Sanjay's specific circumstances (borderline hypertension, overweight BMI, sedentary call-centre job). Education (Sanjay needs information about the link between his lifestyle and his readings, in a format he can act on — because without understanding the connection, he is unlikely to change); strengths-based (asking Sanjay what he enjoys and what small changes he feels able to make builds on his agency rather than imposing a plan); prevention and control (teaching Sanjay to monitor his own blood pressure at home gives him a tool to track his own progress). Considers challenges: Sanjay's sedentary work and possibly limited time for exercise. Uses 'because' and 'therefore'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses at least one strategy with development and some reference to Sanjay.

Developing (2 marks): Names a strategy but limited development; limited link to Sanjay.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a strategy with no development.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which raising awareness through national health campaigns is an effective strategy for promoting health and well-being across the population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation of national campaigns as a health promotion strategy. Strengths: reach — a well-resourced national campaign (e.g. NHS Better Health) can reach millions of people through television, social media and GP signposting, a scale no individual practitioner can match; they raise awareness across the population, meaning even people who do not access health services may be reached; they normalise health-seeking behaviour and positive lifestyle choices. Limitations: awareness does not guarantee behaviour change — knowing that exercise is good does not mean people exercise more; campaigns may not reach the most deprived communities who face structural barriers to health (cost, access, time, housing); they may be more effective for already-motivated individuals and less so for those who need more personalised support. Comparison: campaigns are more effective when combined with local delivery, individual education and strengths-based approaches — the evidence shows that population-level messaging plus individual support is more effective than either alone. Conclusion: national campaigns are a valuable and necessary component of health promotion but are insufficient on their own; their effectiveness is maximised when they are integrated with local and individual-level support.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some development and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Notes some strengths and limitations; limited conclusion.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very brief response.

lessons.title: Health Campaigns, Methods & Current Initiatives
lessons.description: Explore UK health campaigns, their methods, and how to judge whether they work.
lessons.content_html:
Current UK Health Campaigns

The specification requires students to know named, current UK health campaigns across a range of themes. Exam questions often ask students to “name a current campaign” or “give an example of a campaign that promotes [specific health behaviour]” — a vague answer like “a healthy eating campaign” will not score marks. The campaigns below are grouped by theme, as they appear in the specification, and reflect initiatives that are active in the 2025–26 academic year. Note that campaign names change: Change4Life (now NHS Better Health) is one such example — students should know both names.

Campaigns by Theme

Alcohol awareness: Dry January (Alcohol Change UK) runs every January and encourages participants to abstain from alcohol for the month. It has grown significantly since its launch in 2013, with millions of participants annually. Research consistently shows short-term improvements in liver function, blood pressure and sleep quality among participants.

Smoking cessation: No Smoking Day is an annual awareness day held each March, raising awareness of the harms of smoking and signposting support services including NHS Stop Smoking services. It has been running since 1984. Stoptober runs each October and encourages smokers to quit for the month of October, with evidence that those who stop for 28 days are five times more likely to quit for good.

Men’s health: Movember takes place every November, targeting men’s health issues including prostate cancer, testicular cancer, and men’s mental health. By focusing on a visible and engaging activity (sponsored moustache-growing), it reaches men who might not otherwise engage with health services.

Mental health: Time to Talk Day is held each February and is run jointly by Mind and Rethink Mental Illness. It encourages people to have conversations about mental health to reduce stigma and encourage help-seeking. Five Ways to Well-being was developed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) for the government and has been widely adopted by NHS and local authority well-being programmes. The five actions are: connect (with people around you), be active, take notice (of the world around you), keep learning, and give (to others).

Physical activity: Cycle to Work Day encourages employees to cycle to work as a healthy and sustainable commuting choice. It is run in partnership with employers and local authorities. This Girl Can (Sport England) uses authentic, diverse imagery to encourage women and girls to be physically active regardless of their fitness level or body shape, specifically addressing the barriers of self-consciousness and fear of judgement.

Community health and safety: Anti-Bullying Week takes place each November, run by the Anti-Bullying Alliance, promoting positive relationships in schools and online. Keeping Warm in Winter campaigns (coordinated by NHS and local councils) target older adults and those with chronic conditions, reducing the health risks of cold homes including respiratory illness and cardiovascular events. Catch It, Bin It, Kill It is a long-running respiratory hygiene campaign reminding people to catch sneezes and coughs in a tissue and dispose of it promptly, reducing the spread of respiratory infections.

Key Fact

Current named campaigns include: Dry January (alcohol); No Smoking Day and Stoptober (smoking); Movember (men’s health); Time to Talk Day and Five Ways to Well-being (mental health); Cycle to Work Day and This Girl Can (physical activity); Anti-Bullying Week (community). Knowing the campaign name, its theme, and one key feature is the minimum required to score marks.

Methods Used to Deliver Health Campaigns

The specification identifies six main methods through which health campaigns reach their audiences. Understanding each method allows students to evaluate how campaigns are delivered and to assess their likely effectiveness for different target groups.

1. Printed materials (leaflets and posters): Traditional and cost-effective. Leaflets in GP surgeries, pharmacies and community centres reach people at moments when they may be thinking about their health. Posters in public spaces (bus stops, schools, workplaces) build repeated exposure to a message. Limitation: can be ignored, may not reach those with low literacy.

2. Websites and online resources: The NHS and campaign organisations maintain websites with in-depth information, self-assessment tools, and signposting to support services. Websites allow people to access information privately, at a time of their choosing. Limitation: depends on internet access and digital literacy, which are not universal.

3. Television advertisements: Reach a mass audience quickly and can use emotional storytelling to change attitudes. NHS campaigns (including anti-smoking and mental health awareness) have used TV advertising effectively. Limitation: expensive to produce; audiences can skip or tune out.

4. Celebrities, soap operas and drama: Storylines in popular soap operas (such as EastEnders and Emmerdale) have addressed topics including domestic abuse, cancer diagnosis, addiction, and dementia, raising awareness among audiences who might not actively seek health information. Celebrity involvement in campaigns (such as sportspeople promoting exercise or mental health advocates speaking publicly) increases reach and relatability. Limitation: entertainment content is not always factually accurate.

5. Social media, internet and pop-ups: Social media platforms allow campaigns to reach specific demographic groups with targeted messaging. Movember and Time to Talk Day both use social media to encourage sharing and peer-to-peer advocacy. Pop-up adverts on websites and apps can target individuals based on search behaviour. Limitation: algorithm-driven platforms may not reach those most in need; misinformation spreads rapidly online.

6. Guest speakers in schools and colleges: A health professional, service user or campaign representative speaking directly to young people can be more impactful than printed materials, because it allows for questions, personal testimony and two-way dialogue. Limitation: resource-intensive; effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the speaker and session.

Key Fact

The six delivery methods are: printed materials (leaflets, posters); websites; television advertisements; celebrities and soap operas; social media and internet pop-ups; guest speakers in schools and colleges. Each method has different reach, cost, and effectiveness for different target groups.

Reliability and Validity of Health Campaign Information

Not all health information is equally trustworthy. A key skill in health and social care is being able to assess whether information is reliable (consistent, produced by a credible organisation, confirmed by other sources) and valid (accurate, based on sound evidence, and appropriate for the individual).

When evaluating a health campaign, students should consider: who produced the information (is it an NHS body, a recognised charity such as Mind or Cancer Research UK, or a commercial organisation with a financial interest?); what evidence underpins the claims (is it peer-reviewed research, or anecdote?); when it was produced (health guidance changes as new evidence emerges; an older campaign may contain outdated advice); and whether it is appropriate for the target group (a campaign aimed at young men that uses text-heavy leaflets may be less effective than a video on social media).

Compare two sources of information about stopping smoking. Source A is an NHS Better Health Stop Smoking page, citing clinical trials showing the effectiveness of nicotine replacement therapy, updated in 2024 and reviewed by NHS medical advisers. Source B is a blog post by a supplement company recommending a proprietary product to “curb nicotine cravings naturally”, with testimonials but no clinical citations. Source A is more reliable: it is produced by a public health body with no commercial interest, is based on peer-reviewed clinical evidence, and is regularly updated. Source B has lower reliability: the producer has a commercial interest in selling a product, and the evidence is anecdotal rather than clinical. In a care setting, only Source A would be appropriate to share with a service user who wants to stop smoking.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Exam questions on campaigns often ask you to ‘name’ or ‘identify’ a current health campaign — always give the specific name (e.g. Dry January, not just “an alcohol awareness campaign”). For questions about reliability and validity, avoid vague answers like “I would check it is from a good source”. Be specific: name the type of organisation (e.g. NHS, registered charity, government body), the type of evidence (clinical trials rather than testimonials), and the currency of the information (recently updated rather than several years old). The command word ‘Evaluate’ on a campaign question requires you to consider both strengths and limitations of a method or campaign — a one-sided answer cannot reach the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Named current UK campaigns include: Dry January (alcohol), No Smoking Day and Stoptober (smoking), Movember (men’s health), Time to Talk Day and Five Ways to Well-being (mental health), This Girl Can and Cycle to Work Day (physical activity), and Anti-Bullying Week (community). Always learn the campaign name, not just the theme.
  • Six delivery methods are used by campaigns: printed materials, websites, television advertising, celebrities and soap operas, social media and pop-ups, and guest speakers in schools and colleges. Each has strengths and limitations.
  • Reliable and valid health information comes from NHS bodies, registered charities, and government organisations, is underpinned by clinical evidence, is recently updated, and is appropriate for the target group. Always consider who produced the information and why.

practice_questions.text: Explain why social media is used as a method of delivering health campaigns to young people.

practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for accurately describing Five Ways to Well-being (a framework developed by the New Economics Foundation identifying five evidence-based actions to improve well-being: connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, and give [1]; adopted by NHS and public health bodies as a well-being promotion tool [1]). Up to 2 marks for a specific, plausible practitioner example (e.g. a community nurse working with an isolated older adult could use the 'connect' action to encourage them to join a local social group, because social connection is an evidence-based way to improve mental well-being and reduce loneliness [1]; the nurse discusses which of the five actions the service user finds most realistic given their circumstances, applying the framework in a person-centred way [1]).

practice_questions.text:
Devika is 45 years old and is looking for information online about whether she should take a particular herbal supplement that claims to reduce blood pressure. She has found two sources: one from the NHS website and one from a blog run by the supplement manufacturer.

Discuss how Devika could assess the reliability and validity of each source of information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Applies reliability and validity criteria specifically to both sources with developed reasoning. NHS website: produced by a public health body with no commercial interest in a particular product [1]; information is based on clinical evidence reviewed by medical professionals [1]; content is regularly updated, so advice reflects current guidance [1]. Supplement manufacturer's blog: commercial interest — the producer benefits financially from promoting the supplement [1]; evidence may be based on customer testimonials rather than clinical trials, which is less reliable [1]; information may not be reviewed by qualified health professionals and may be out of date or selectively presented [1]. Overall assessment: Devika should rely on the NHS source for accurate guidance on managing blood pressure; the manufacturer's source is less valid because it may not accurately reflect the full clinical picture [1].

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses both sources with some reliability/validity analysis; at least two developed points.

Developing (2 marks): Addresses one source or gives a very general answer about reliability.

Emerging (1 mark): Identifies one source as more reliable without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively the method of using celebrities and soap opera storylines promotes health and well-being across different groups in the population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation addressing specific strengths and limitations of using celebrities and soap opera storylines as a campaign delivery method, with reference to different population groups. Strengths: reaches large audiences who do not actively seek health information — soap opera viewers include older adults, families and young people across social backgrounds; emotional storytelling can change attitudes more effectively than information alone because audiences empathise with characters; a celebrity speaking openly about mental health (e.g. a public figure discussing depression) can normalise help-seeking, particularly among groups (e.g. men) who are reluctant to admit vulnerability; evidence from mental health charities shows that soap opera storylines (e.g. suicide storylines handled responsibly) lead to increased calls to support services in the following days. Limitations: not always factually accurate — entertainment takes precedence over precision; not all groups watch television or follow specific celebrities — younger people, recent migrants and those without mainstream media access may not be reached; messages delivered indirectly through storylines may not be specific enough to enable individual action; celebrities who endorse products commercially may reduce public trust. Evaluation of effectiveness by group: effective for older adults (high soap viewing rates) and for reducing stigma around mental health (Time to Talk); less effective for reaching those not represented in mainstream media. Conclusion: celebrity and soap methods are effective for reaching broad audiences and changing attitudes, but they should be combined with targeted local delivery methods (e.g. guest speakers, social media) to reach groups underserved by mainstream media.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some group differentiation and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Addresses some strengths and limitations; limited differentiation by group.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very general response.
